title: The Lord stood to finish the work
word: The Lord stood to finish the work
hook: the Lord Himself stood to complete the saints' task, sung of the pool at Amritsar (Suhi M5, ang 783)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mundavani, the plate that seals the Granth. Your line was truth, contentment, reflection. Which of the three did your meal remind you of? Day one thousand two hundred nine.

Dig a hole by hand and there comes a moment. Shovel after shovel, the pile grows, and the hole seems to shrink. Then someone climbs down beside you and takes the other end. In Raga Suhi, on Ang seven hundred eighty-three, Guru Arjan sings about a great work of digging and building: the pool at Amritsar, the work tradition says his father, Guru Ram Das, began. And the song doesn't say, look what we built. It says something stranger. The Lord stood up to do it.
screen: `SHOVEL AFTER SHOVEL.` → `THE POOL AT AMRITSAR.` → `THE LORD STOOD UP TO DO IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, paraphrased: for the task of the saints, the Lord Himself stood up; He came to have the work done. Khaloiaa, stood up, is a picture word. Not watched from far off. Not sent help. Stood, the way a person gets up from where they were sitting when the work in front of them matters. The hymn goes on, again paraphrased: the land is beautiful, the pool is beautiful, filled with nectar water. Sikh tradition sings it of the pool at Amritsar, the pool around which the Harmandir Sahib stands. Now look at who gets the credit. Tradition remembers builders and diggers and the sangat carrying earth: real people doing real labor. The hymn doesn't deny it. It just says whose hand was underneath theirs. The saints had the task. The Lord stood to finish it. Sikh teaching holds both of these at once, and this path has been circling the same idea. The Bavan Akhri ended in grace. The Mundavani laid the Name on the plate as the support of all. Here, the same truth is wearing work clothes. It's dusty. It has a shovel. Effort is honored, and then the one who completes it is named. Some readers hear this hymn as permission to be finished. Not because you got it all done alone, but because you weren't alone in it.
screen: `THE LORD HIMSELF STOOD UP.` · `KHALOIAA: A PICTURE WORD.` · `THE POOL FILLED WITH NECTAR.` · `REAL LABOR, AND THE HAND BENEATH IT.` · then, large: `HE FINISHED IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish a task with help. Bring to mind one task you've been carrying alone, half-dug. Sit with it for a moment. Then ask honestly who could take the other end of the shovel: a friend, a coworker, a family member. Think about asking them. If you pray, you can hold the task before Waheguru and leave it there for a breath. When the sit is over, if you can, send one message asking for help. The bell holds the time.
The Lord stood to finish the work. For the saints' task, Guru Arjan sings, the Lord Himself stood up; sung of the pool at Amritsar. Today's word.
screen: `THE LORD STOOD TO FINISH THE WORK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: he finished it. Today, when something you worked on comes together, say thank you to someone who helped, and let yourself notice the hand underneath yours. Day one thousand two hundred nine.

howItsDone: This hymn of Guru Arjan in Raga Suhi is sung in kirtan, and some Sikhs connect it with the sarovar at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar and with seva done there.
